Consider if the patient is systemically unwell, very frail, has comorbidity (COPD, heart failure), or pertussis is suspected (macrolide).

| Heart failure (pulmonary oedema) | Orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, rapid onset dyspnoea | BNP elevated, chest X‑ray shows Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly; cough is usually dry, not productive mucus‑laden |
Side effects: reduced appetite, insomnia, increased heart rate and blood pressure, slowed growth in children (monitor height and weight), potential for misuse.
Medically ill patients: Adjust for kidney and liver disease; check heart disease and QT prolongation; consider interactions with other drugs.

| Heart failure (pulmonary oedema) | Orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, elevated JVP; bilateral basal crackles; BNP high; CXR shows Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly | Cardiovascular signs, response to diuretics, no focal consolidation on CXR |
Review at 48 hours; if no improvement, think of empyema, resistant or unusual organism, TB, obstruction (cancer), wrong diagnosis (PE, heart failure).

qs.q: KOH examination of sputum from a heart transplant patient with fever and pulmonary infiltrates shows oval budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae. What is the diagnostic significance?
o: Highly indicative of a fungal infection, likely Candidiasis.
qs.e: The presence of oval budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae in a KOH preparation of sputum is highly indicative of a fungal infection, most commonly Candidiasis, especially in an immunocompromised patient like a heart transplant recipient.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Virology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 55-year-old man with heart failure has a right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis shows fluid protein of 2.1 g/dL, serum protein 7.0 g/dL, fluid LDH 88 U/L, and serum LDH 300 U/L. Most likely type of effusion?
qs.e: Using Light's criteria: (1) Fluid protein/serum protein ratio (2.1/7.0 = 0.3) is <0.5. (2) Fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio (88/300 = 0.29) is <0.6. (3) Fluid LDH (88 U/L) is <2/3 the upper limit of normal for serum LDH (typically ~200 U/L, so 2/3 of 300 is 200). All criteria point to a transudate, consistent with heart failure.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman with no cardiopulmonary disease has progressive exertional dyspnea, syncope on exertion, and loud P2 on auscultation. Right heart catheterization shows mean pulmonary artery pressure of 38 mmHg with normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Progressive exertional dyspnea, syncope on exertion, and a loud P2 are suggestive of pulmonary hypertension. The right heart catheterization findings of elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure (38 mmHg) with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (indicating no left heart failure) confirm pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension, most consistent with Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH).

qs.q: A 16-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. BP barely obtainable, lungs clear, heart sounds barely audible. Most useful treatment?
qs.e: The presentation of barely obtainable blood pressure, clear lungs, and barely audible heart sounds after a chest stab wound is highly suggestive of cardiac tamponade. Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax. Intravenous fluids may help but are insufficient alone. qs.q: A 72-year-old man with heart failure receives two units of packed red cells. During the second unit he develops dyspnea, hypertension, and an elevated JVP. CXR shows pulmonary edema. Most likely transfusion complication?
qs.e: Dyspnea + hypertension + elevated JVP + pulmonary edema in a patient with heart failure after transfusion = TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload). Unlike TRALI, TACO is cardiogenic and patients have elevated filling pressures. Treated with diuretics.

qs.q: What percentage of Down syndrome patients have congenital heart disease?
qs.e: Approximately 40% of Down syndrome patients have congenital heart disease, most commonly endocardial cushion defects including atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.

qs.q: A 44-year-old woman dies of a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She has LVH (550g heart), small scarred kidneys, and arterioles with concentric intimal thickening. Most likely condition?
qs.e: LVH + CNS hemorrhage + small kidneys + hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis = malignant hypertension with multi-organ end-organ damage.

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease receives a porcine bioprosthesis. After 10 years it needs replacement. Most likely pathologic finding?
qs.e: Bioprosthetic valves avoid anticoagulation but undergo progressive calcification over 5–10 years, causing stenosis and requiring replacement.

es.q: A patient presents with acute liver injury secondary to severe right heart failure. Which acinar zone would you expect to be most affected and why?
es.m: Zone 3 (centrilobular) would be most affected. This zone has the worst oxygenation, making it highly susceptible to ischemic injury, as seen in conditions like right heart failure.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A 55-year-old male presents with signs of severe right heart failure. Which acinar zone is most likely to be affected by the resulting hepatic congestion and ischemia, and what is its characteristic oxygenation status?
es.m: Zone 3 (Centrilobular) is most likely to be affected. This zone is characterized by the worst oxygenation due to its location furthest from the portal triads and direct proximity to the central vein, making it highly susceptible to ischemic injury.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A patient presents with hepatic injury secondary to severe right heart failure. Which acinar zone would you expect to be primarily affected on histological examination, and what is the pathophysiological basis for this vulnerability?
es.m: Zone 3 (centrilobular) would be primarily affected. This zone is the furthest from the portal triads and thus receives the poorest oxygenation. In severe right heart failure, hepatic venous congestion leads to reduced blood flow and oxygen delivery, making Zone 3 particularly susceptible to hypoxic damage.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A patient with suspected liver dysfunction presents with severe right heart failure. Based on the liver's acinar organization, which specific zone is most vulnerable to injury in this scenario, and what are its characteristic features and oxygenation status?
es.m: In a patient with severe right heart failure, the most vulnerable zone is Zone 3, also known as the centrilobular zone. This zone is characterized by the worst oxygenation due to its farthest proximity from the portal triad's hepatic artery supply. It is specifically affected by conditions causing ischemia, shock, and right heart failure.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

ai.summary: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump located in the middle mediastinum. It consists of two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers). The wall comprises three layers: the outer epicardium (visceral pericardium), the thick muscular myocardium, and the inner endocardium.

sections.p: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump located in the middle mediastinum. It consists of two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers). The wall comprises three layers: the outer epicardium (visceral pericardium), the thick muscular myocardium, and the inner endocardium.

b: Apex: Formed by the left ventricle, located in the 5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Base: Primarily formed by the left atrium, facing posteriorly.
Sternocostal (Anterior) Surface: Mainly formed by the right ventricle.
Diaphragmatic (Inferior) Surface: Formed by both ventricles, primarily the left.
Atrioventricular (AV) Valves: Tricuspid (right) and Mitral (left). Supported by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles to prevent regurgitation during systole.
Semilunar Valves: Pulmonary and Aortic. These prevent backflow from the great vessels during diastole.
Right Coronary Artery (RCA): Supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, SA node (60%), and AV node (80%).
Left Coronary Artery (LCA): Divides into the Left Anterior Descending (LAD), supplying the anterior septum and apex, and the Circumflex artery, supplying the left atrium and posterior left ventricle.

sections.p: Understanding heart anatomy is essential for interpreting Chest X-rays (cardiac silhouette) and diagnosing conditions like heart failure, valvular heart disease, and myocardial infarction.

b: Auricles vs Atria: Auricles are small, muscular pouches projecting from the atria, while atria are the main receiving chambers.
Right vs Left Ventricle walls: The left ventricle is three times thicker than the right to overcome high systemic vascular resistance.
Dextrocardia: In this congenital condition, the heart is mirrored on the right side, which can lead to incorrect electrode placement during ECGs.
Referred pain: Cardiac ischemia often presents as pain in the left arm or jaw due to shared spinal cord segments (T1-T5).

faq.q: What defines the 'base' of the heart?
faq.a: The base is the posterior aspect, formed mainly by the left atrium and a small part of the right atrium, facing the vertebrae.

faq.q: Which coronary artery is usually dominant?
faq.a: The right coronary artery is dominant in approximately 70% of people, meaning it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.

faq.q: Where is the apex beat normally palpated?
faq.a: It is typically found in the left fifth intercostal space, along the midclavicular line.
